lines.text: Why do some collisions between reactant particles lead to products while others do not? A collision must meet an energy threshold.

Activation energy, E ay, is the minimum energy required for a collision to be effective. Particles in a sample do not all have the same energy. A collision whose energy is below E ay is ineffective, one that reaches this threshold can be effective. The definition concerns the collision, not the average energy of the sample. Prerequisite bridge, an effective collision from eight point one forms products, simply counting all collisions includes encounters that lack enough energy or a suitable orientation.
Use this threshold on a Boltzmann distribution, particles to the right of E A have sufficient energy to react.
E ay, minimum energy required for a collision to be effective. Collisions below E A are ineffective. The threshold belongs to the reaction pathway.
Define E A precisely, then explain why a collision below it cannot produce reaction.
At one temperature, why are only some particles energetic enough to react? The Boltzmann distribution displays their range of energies.

That increased area explains why heating makes effective collisions more frequent.

Horizontal axis, molecular energy, vertical axis, number or proportion of molecules. Area under curve, total number or proportion. Area right of E ay, particles with sufficient energy. Heating lowers and shifts the peak right while preserving total area.
Sketch two temperature curves for the same sample and explain why their areas beyond E A differ.
A modest temperature rise can markedly speed a reaction. The important change is how many collisions meet the energy threshold.

Increasing temperature gives particles greater average kinetic energy and broadens the Boltzmann distribution towards higher energies. The fraction with energy at least E A rises, even though E A remains unchanged for the same pathway. Particles also move faster and collide somewhat more often. Most importantly, a larger fraction of collisions is effective, so the frequency of effective collisions increases and the reaction rate rises. Cooling reverses these changes, the fraction beyond E ay, frequency of effective collisions and rate all fall. Prerequisite bridge, use the tail area from eight point two point two as the fraction meeting the energy condition, then connect this with the frequency of effective collisions from eight point one. Explain the rate, rather than predicting an equilibrium yield.
Distinguish this temperature effect from increasing concentration, which chiefly raises collision frequency, and from a catalyst, which lowers the threshold through an alternative pathway.

Heating broadens the Boltzmann distribution towards high energies. More particles have energy at least E ay. Effective collisions occur more frequently, increasing rate. Cooling produces the reverse effect.

eight point two Effect of temperature on reaction rates and the concept of activation energy.
In one breath.
Heating spreads molecular energies towards higher values. More collisions then meet the activation energy threshold, so the frequency of effective collisions and the reaction rate increase.
Key ideas.

Activation energy, E ay, is the minimum energy required for a collision to be effective. A collision below this energy cannot produce reaction. It is a threshold for a particular reaction pathway, not the energy carried by every particle. At a fixed temperature, particles have different energies, so only some collisions meet the threshold.

The Boltzmann distribution describes the distribution of molecular energies in a sample. The horizontal axis is molecular energy and the vertical axis is the number or proportion of molecules with that energy. The curve starts at the origin, rises to a peak at the most probable energy, then tails away towards high energy. The area under the whole curve represents the total number of molecules, or a total proportion of one. For the same sample, that total area is constant. The area under the curve to the right of a vertical E A line represents particles with enough energy to react, it is an energy condition, not a guarantee that every such particle reacts on its next collision.

When temperature increases, the distribution broadens. Its peak becomes lower and moves right, towards higher energy, the high energy tail contains a greater proportion of molecules. The total area stays the same because no particles have been added. The E A line stays in the same place for an unchanged pathway. Hence the area to its right grows substantially.
Method.
To sketch and use a Boltzmann distribution.
Label molecular energy on the horizontal axis and number or proportion of molecules on the vertical axis. Start each curve at the origin and let its high energy tail approach the axis.
For a higher temperature, draw a lower, broader peak farther to the right. Keep the total area the same. A lower temperature curve is taller, narrower and peaks farther left.
Draw the same vertical E A line for both temperatures. Compare the areas under each curve to its right. The higher temperature area is larger.
Translate the area comparison into collisions, a larger fraction of collisions has energy at least E ay, so effective collisions occur more frequently and the rate rises.
Worked example.

A gas reaction is heated without changing the reactants or catalyst. Sketch the new energy distribution and explain the faster rate. Draw molecular energy horizontally and number of molecules vertically. Keep the original curve for comparison. Add a curve with a lower peak farther right and a broader tail, preserve its total area. Keep the E A line fixed. Shade or identify the increased area to its right. More particles have energy at least E ay and therefore the frequency of effective collisions increases. Faster moving particles may also collide more frequently, but the increase in the fraction above E ay is the main explanation.
Traps.
Trap, Heating lowers activation energy. Why it's wrong, Temperature changes particle energies, not the threshold of the unchanged pathway. Instead, Keep E A fixed and change the distribution.
Trap, A hotter sample has a taller peak. Why it's wrong, The energies are more spread out while the total number stays constant. Instead, Draw a lower, broader peak shifted right.

Trap, Rate rises only because particles collide more often. Why it's wrong, This misses the much larger change in the fraction with sufficient energy. Instead, State that the frequency of effective collisions rises because more collisions exceed E ay.
Exam technique.

For Define, use the exact phrase minimum energy required for a collision to be effective. For Sketch, show the origin, axes, peak positions, high energy tails, equal total areas and unchanged E ay. For Explain, connect temperature to the Boltzmann distribution, then to the proportion above E ay, then to effective collision frequency and rate. Do not say that every particle gains the same amount of energy. If a catalyst is mentioned, distinguish its lower energy pathway from a temperature change.
